Notes
Note that

The pure spline fit fits the training data better (it interpolates it), but fits the (unseen) test data worse.
In contrast, the ODE-penalised fit fits the training data worse but generalises to unseen data better.

This is a common phenomenon! For this and related reasons, statisticians and modellers have traditionally advised against exactly fitting the training data in the name of avoiding overfitting.
However, the main concern is not so much having ‘too good’ of a fit to the training data, rather the concern that this may not be representative of the ability to fit the test data.
One of the more surprising observations of modern machine learning is there are models that exactly fit the training data and yet generalise well to new data. One perspective on this is that away from data points the regularisation or structural assumptions dominate, and that it is possible to both fit the training data well and generalise well, if we also have good regularisation/structural assumptions.
In the present course, however, we will typically see the traditional wisdom – of sacrificing some fit to the training data in order to get better fit to unseen data – hold up.
This relates to the topic of\(\dots\)

title: Hybrid models
text:
Choosing regularisation parameters
So far we have pre-specified the regularisation parameter. In both the pseudo-inverse and physics-informed cases we have general guidelines for setting this: for the pseudo-inverse we set it to be ‘small but not zero’. For a physics model we set it to be ‘large’ if we think the model is correct. What about in general? Can we use the data to determine a ‘good’ value?
One issue is that \(\lambda\) controls the ability to fit unseen data: it involves a loss term evaluated at points other than the training data (e.g. the fine time scale). If we fit its value based just on the training data, and the data model component is capable of fitting the training data exactly, the optimal value will be zero (why?)!
A strategy around this, is to set regularisation/generalisation/hyperparameters like \(\lambda\) based on the ability of the fitted model to predict data it wasn’t trained on. The simplest way to do this is to split our original training dataset into a smaller training data subset and a non-overlapping validation subset (you will have seen this idea already!). We fit the model on the training subset for various \(\lambda\) values and use these models to predict the unfitted validation set. We use the \(\lambda\) value that leads to the best predicting model. This mimics the process of fitting a model to training data and evaluating on test data, and hence provides information about ‘generalisation’ ability (under assumptions such as exchangeable or IID data, however!).
This approach falls under the umbrella of the family of techniques known as cross-validation. More sophisticated variations of cross-validation, such as \(k\)-fold cross-validation, repeatedly split the training data into training and validation data subsets and assess the average performance on the validation sets. Note that we typically still have a third, separate test set that we don’t see until the final model, including hyperparameters, is developed.
Other approaches, popular in inverse problems (see ENGSCI 721), include L-curves and discrepancy principles.

Data splitting for choosing \(\lambda\)
The same splitting schemes from the first half of the course apply here. The figure below compares a single training/validation split with five-fold cross-validation for choosing \(\lambda\). We then consider how to form the splits to reflect the prediction task, including preserving subgroup proportions and using past and present observations to predict future values.







Figure 1: As indicated in the figure, we use the training data to determine the weights for each candidate \(\lambda\) (within-model inference), and the validation data to determine which \(\lambda\) to use (model selection). We then keep the chosen \(\lambda\) fixed and refit the weights using all the training and validation data, before evaluating the fitted model on the test set.




Keeping subgroup proportions similar
We can form stratified folds so that chosen categories or subgroups appear in approximately the same proportions as in the data being split. Suppose we are predicting property prices from 100 sales: 80 detached houses and 20 apartments. A stratified five-fold split could put 16 houses and 4 apartments in each fold, so that we calculate validation errors on data with the same mixture of property types as the original dataset.
There is no universally best way to stratify, and the choice depends on the target population we wish to predict for and the type of prediction task we want to assess. Keeping subgroup proportions similar can make validation scores less sensitive to the particular split. However, when we interpret those scores as performance on the target population, we are assuming that our sample is representative. For example, our 80:20 mixture of houses and apartments might have arisen partly by chance and differ from the population we want to predict for. In this case, our validation scores would give more or less weight to the prediction errors for apartments vs. houses than they would in a more representative sample.


Predicting future values
The figure below compares predicting new cases from the same population with predicting future values from earlier observations.






Figure 2: For new cases, we fit using the blue observations and evaluate predictions on the held-out orange observations. For future prediction, we fit using observations available at the cutoff and evaluate predictions at later times. When choosing \(\lambda\), we repeat the fitting and prediction for each candidate value and compare these validation errors.



While a random or stratified split can suit independent observations from the same population, for time-series prediction we often want to represent the ‘online’ nature of the task, where we only have access to past and present observations when predicting the future. We therefore fit using earlier observations and validate at later times. In Lab 4, we use the held-out later part of the reference trajectory to choose \(\lambda\). This explicitly checks our ability to predict beyond the fitting interval into the future, whereas withholding points within that interval can test interpolation or smoothing using observations on both sides.
We can repeat the early/later split as new observations become available. In rolling-origin evaluation, we move the prediction cutoff forward, refit using the observations then available, and predict the next interval. The figure below shows an expanding training window, with the same prediction horizon at each step.






Figure 3: At each cutoff, we fit using the blue observations and predict the following orange interval. After those outcomes become available, we evaluate the predictions, advance the cutoff and refit. Observations used for validation in an earlier row can then be used for fitting in a later row. Grey blocks lie beyond the prediction interval for that row.



Later fits in this scheme use more observations. The errors can change both because we have more training data and because we are predicting a different part of the series. Averaging the errors summarises performance across these cutoffs, rather than the performance of one final fit using all available observations.
To compare candidate \(\lambda\) values, we use the same cutoffs and prediction horizon for every candidate and choose \(\lambda\) using the average validation error. We choose the first cutoff so that there are enough earlier observations to fit the model. If a final test interval is reserved, it stays outside these repeated validation checks.
If the prediction task instead uses a fixed amount of recent history, we can move a fixed-width training window forward, so that each fit uses the same number of earlier observations.

title: Hybrid models
text:
Generalised cross-validation for linear models
Generally, the more complex the model (e.g. deep neural network vs linear model), the simpler the data splitting approach is, as it can be hard/computationally expensive to implement more sophisticated methods.
For linear models, however, there is a particularly simple approximation available: generalised cross-validation. This is somewhat of a misnomer: it is an approximation to what you would obtain by carrying out ‘leave-one-out’ cross-validation for a linear model.
For time-series data, a leave-one-out fit can use observations on both sides of the omitted point. The chronological splits above instead assess prediction into the future using only earlier observations.
You don’t need to know the details, but for completeness, it minimises the following formula (representing generalisation error) to estimate \(\lambda\): \[
\text{GCV}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{m} \frac{\| (I - H_{\lambda}) y_{\text{obs}} \|^2}{\left( 1 - \frac{\text{Tr}(H_{\lambda})}{m} \right)^2}
\] where \(m\) is the number of observations and \(H_{\lambda}\) is the hat (smoothing) matrix associated with the regularised estimate. For our hybrid model, when the stacked system has full column rank, this is given by: \[
H_{\lambda} = B_{\text{obs}} \left( B_{\text{obs}}^T B_{\text{obs}} + \lambda B^T D^T D B \right)^{-1} B_{\text{obs}}^T
\] where \(B_{\text{obs}} = A_{\text{obs}}B\) and \(D\) is the matrix used in the penalty (\(D_3\) in the example below). In the code below, we calculate this matrix using the augmented least squares solver rather than forming the inverse.
The important point is that, although it may look intimidating, this is easy to calculate for linear models for each \(\lambda\). We can simply evaluate this for a grid of \(\lambda\) values and choose the one giving the smallest value.

title: Neural networks
text:
Artificial intelligence and neural networks: brief history
Artificial intelligence (AI), of which ‘machine learning’ is a subfield, has undergone numerous ‘booms’ and ‘busts’ since around 1950. The term AI winter has been used for several of the ‘bust’ cycles in AI, where funding and interest dropped after failures to live up to the hype. This includes ‘bust’ periods such as 1974-1980 and 1987-2000. The current ‘boom’ period (as of 2026) roughly started around 2012. (See e.g. the Wikipedia article AI Winter for further reading and references.)
Within AI, neural networks have undergone their own boom and bust periods. For example, after their initial hype (see NY Times article!), Minsky and Papert published a book Perceptrons in 1969 containing several criticisms of neural networks. Famously, they showed that single-layer neural nets are unable to compute the basic logical operation XOR (exclusive OR). It was known that multiple-layer networks (called multilayer networks or multilayer perceptrons) were not subject to this limitation, but feasible training methods for these were not known. In contrast, many AI researchers between the 1950s and 1980s focused on expert systems and symbolic AI, in which explicit rules are encoded rather than learned from data (note the similarity to encoding ‘engineering knowledge’!)

title: Neural networks
text: The book that (briefly) killed neural networks??

title: Neural networks
section: Artificial intelligence and neural networks: brief history continued
text:
Artificial intelligence and neural networks: brief history continued
Development of the backpropagation algorithm for training multilayer neural networks helped lead to renewed interest in neural networks in the 1980s. Backpropagation – essentially efficiently and automatically using the chain rule to compute gradients and hence carry out optimisation – was popularised in the 1980s, for example in the 1986 paper Learning representations by back-propagating errors by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams. However, it wasn’t until around 2012 that the availability of cheap and powerful computer hardware like GPUs, the availability of large datasets, and better architectures and training methods for older ideas such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), enabled the current explosion of interest (currently the ‘hot’ architecture is the transformer, the ‘T’ in ChatGPT!). These advances have led to a resurgence in machine learning and the use of neural networks with many- (many, many-) layers, often referred to as deep neural networks. Training such networks is known as deep learning.
Machine learning is an opposing but complementary approach to rule-based AI – a yin and yang! The idea is to learn approximate, statistical, rules from the data, rather than impose them a priori. As we have seen, this has strengths and weaknesses in engineering applications! For now, engineers appear to need to continue to learn the ‘rules’ of Newton’s Laws of motion alongside machine learning and statistics. Perhaps, however, we will see the machine learning approach continue to supplant traditional approaches? Or perhaps various hybrid methods, such as those we looked at in the previous section, will come to dominate? Exciting times!
So far we have fitted models to time series, such as a pendulum’s angle over time, including hybrid models that build in physics. In this chapter we introduce neural networks through basic image classification: recognising handwritten digits. In the next chapter we return to time series prediction and hybrid modelling, with a neural network as the data model.

title: Neural networks
text:
Neural networks vs linear models
What is a neural network? First consider a simple linear model for observations \((x_i,y_i)\), \(i=1,\dots,m\), \[y_i \approx b + x_i w \]
where \(w\) is a weight parameter and \(b\) is called a bias parameter (or intercept in linear regression). This can also be written as
\[y_i \approx 1 b + x_i w = \begin{bmatrix}1 & x_i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}b\\ w\end{bmatrix}\] where we include the ‘constant feature’ 1. For \(m\) observations we get the vector equation
\[
y = \bar{X} \bar{w}
\] where \[
\bar{X} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_1\\
1 & x_2\\
\vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x_m
\end{bmatrix}
\] and \[\bar{w} = \begin{bmatrix}b\\ w\end{bmatrix}.\] We’ve used a ‘bar’ over the \(X\) and \(w\) to indicate the constant/bias terms are included. For various reasons, neural network folk often keep the weights and bias terms separate, and instead write e.g.  \[
y = 1_mb + Xw
\] where here \[
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2\\
\vdots\\
x_m
\end{bmatrix}
\] and \(1_m\) is a ones vector of length \(m\).

title: Neural networks
text:
Neural networks vs linear models
So far we have a standard linear model. This can obviously be extended to multiple input features, e.g. if we denote the \(i\)th measurement of the \(j\)th feature as \(x_{ij}\) we have a design/feature matrix of the form: \[
X = [x_{ij}]_{i=1:m,j=1:n}
\] and linear model \[
y \approx b1_m +  Xw
\] for feature weights \[
w = \begin{bmatrix}w_1\\w_2\\\vdots\\w_n\end{bmatrix}
\] The neural network folk like to represent this model with diagrams like the below: 
The bias term is sometimes depicted explicitly but often left implicit. We almost have a simple neural network! We just need one more element that is normally implied by diagrams like the above\(\dots\)

title: Neural networks
text:
Activation functions
The main element distinguishing a neural network from a standard linear model is a nonlinearity introduced by an activation function applied to the output of a linear component before the final output is produced. This means our model for a single output has the general form: \[
y \approx f(Xw + 1_mb)
\] where \(f\) is a nonlinear function called an activation function that is (usually) applied elementwise, i.e. to each sample realisation, so that \[
y_i \approx f(\text{row}_i(X)w + b)
\] where \(\text{row}_i(X)\) is the \(i\)th row of \(X\). Activation functions were originally inspired by the behaviour of biological neurons, which typically only ‘fire’ (send a signal) when a threshold signal is reached. Thus, typical activation functions generally have a threshold or switch-like shape, with varying degrees of smoothness and saturation properties, e.g.



Typical activation functions, where \(z\) is the output of the linear component.


Although originally inspired by biology, mathematically, the important thing is that introducing nonlinearities allows us to represent more complex classes of functions: so-called universal approximation theorems state, roughly, that sufficiently complex neural networks, with nonlinear activation functions, can approximate any continuous function on a bounded range of inputs as closely as we like, given enough neurons. These theorems say that suitable weights exist; they don’t say that training will find them, or how much data that takes.

title: Neural networks
text:
Multiple neurons and multiple layers
So far we have a single ‘regression’ style equation that represents a single output given multiple features, a weight for each feature, a single bias term, and a nonlinearity applied to the output of the linear component. This is called an artificial neuron, or just neuron for short. Similar models occur in statistics, for example this class of models essentially corresponds to so-called generalised linear models in statistics. What else distinguishes neural networks from standard statistical models?
Another key element in neural networks is that we typically consider multiple neurons, arranged in layers, as in the below diagram. There are three types of layers: input, output, and the intermediate hidden layers. Note, however, that we can have as many hidden layers as we want!



Neural network with one hidden layer


Thus we have a collection of regression-like equations that in turn form the features for another collection of regression-like equations, and so on, until we reach the output. Note, though: without nonlinear activation functions this would still just be a big linear model!

title: Neural networks
text:
Architecture
The term architecture refers to the structural design of the neural network: how many layers, how many neurons – also called nodes or units – in each layer, etc. The number of layers is referred to as the depth, while the number of neurons in a layer is referred to as the (layer) width.
A feedforward neural network is the archetypal neural network where information moves in only one direction – from the input nodes, through the hidden layers, and finally to the output nodes (as in the diagram above). There are no loops or feedback connections between nodes in the network. Hence its general architecture consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer:





Recurrent neural networks include ‘recurrent connections’ or loops and are hence no longer feedforward neural networks. For simplicity we only focus on very simple feedforward neural networks here. It is relatively simple to experiment with different architectures in PyTorch on your own, however!

title: Neural networks
section: How many layers? Deep learning and feature engineering
text:
How many layers? Deep learning and feature engineering
Since around 2012 there has been a large shift towards increasing deep architectures with many layers. Why? What’s the goal? The following image from ‘Deep Learning with PyTorch’ by Stevens, Antiga, and Viehmann (2020) illustrates the conceptual shift associated with deep learning vs. more ‘traditional’ machine learning/data science:









Feature engineering







Deep learning





That is, in theory, the goal of deep learning is to automatically learn as much of the data-to-outcome pipeline as possible, reducing the reliance on hand-crafted components. Note, however, that this diagram just illustrates the general conceptual orientation of different approaches, and is not a prescription of what to do. As engineers, we have professional and ethical obligations in terms of safety and reliability, as well as a pragmatic orientation on timely results. Current deep learning pipelines may not be the safest/most reliable/timely approach for many engineering applications!

title: Neural networks
text:
Building neural networks in PyTorch
So far we’ve mainly just used the tensor data structures available in PyTorch, and a little of its autodiff capabilities. In theory, we could build neural networks from these components. However, the main torch module of PyTorch also contains a submodule torch.nn dedicated to helping us build neural networks more easily.
There are two main ways to build neural networks in PyTorch. The simplest is to use the further submodule of nn, torch.nn.Sequential, which allows us to simply specify a sequence of ‘layers’ to define a neural network model. While we can use this to do familiar things like predict the motion of a pendulum or projectile, we can also use this approach to make a simple neural network for image classification. For example, here is a simple neural network designed to classify \(28 \times 28\) pixel grayscale images into one of five classes:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Define the model
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, 5),
    nn.Softmax(dim=1)
)

That’s it! Sort of\(\dots\) we still need to obtain our training data and train our model. But first, let’s consider what’s happening in our model.

title: Neural networks
text:
Terminology
Note on terminology: Flatten, ReLU and Softmax are considered ‘layers’ in the PyTorch model, but these are not parameterised. They instead represent data reshaping, data transformations, and activation functions. In standard, mathematical neural network terminology we usually only use the term ‘layer’ for what we would call parameterised layers in PyTorch (other than the input/data layer which is not parameterised).
Furthermore, in a PyTorch ‘layer’ like nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128), its mathematical/diagrammatic counterpart is associated with the output nodes (128) of the PyTorch layer. So the width of the layer in the mathematical/diagrammatic sense is 128. Here we have five PyTorch ‘layers’ corresponding, in standard neural network terms, to one input layer and two (parameterised) layers. That is, we have one (non-parameterised) input layer, one (parameterised) hidden layer, and one (parameterised) output layer. There are also multiple output classes.



Neural network predicting multiple class probabilities.

title: Neural networks
text:
Input layer
The first ‘layer’ (in PyTorch terms) is nn.Flatten. This turns each image into a vector by ‘flattening’ the image row-wise into a long vector:



Turning an image into a vector.


Note that a common mathematical convention (and the Fortran convention) is to flatten column-wise, but NumPy and PyTorch, following C, flatten row-wise by default.
This step is needed because nn.Linear acts on the last dimension of its input. Flattening puts all \(28 \times 28 = 784\) pixel values of each image in that dimension, so a minibatch becomes a tensor of shape [batch_size, 784], with one row per image and the pixel values as its ‘features’. Note though, that other, more advanced image-handling layers (such as convolutional layers) do not require images to be flattened, and can work directly with multi-dimensional tensors.
This is a non-parameterised layer and is essentially our input layer.

title: Neural networks
text:
Hidden layers
The nn.Linear PyTorch layer is the first parameterised layer of the neural network and is a hidden layer because its output nodes are not directly observed outputs.
This layer has \(28 \times 28 = 784\) input nodes and 128 output nodes. That is, we are representing 128 ‘regressions’, each taking 784 input variables with their own weights! Each regression also has a bias term, so we get \(128 \times 784 + 128 = 100480\) learnable parameters. The width of this layer is 128, i.e. the number of output nodes in the layer.
The layer’s weights form a \(784\times128\) matrix \(W\), with one row per input pixel and one column per neuron, and its biases a vector \(b\) of length 128. Each column of \(W\) holds one neuron’s 784 weights, like the weight vector \(w\) in the linear models chapter: placing the 128 regressions side by side gives \(W\). As in that chapter, observations go in rows, so for a minibatch \(X\) with one flattened image per row the layer computes \(XW+b\) (the convention of Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville’s Deep Learning):



The weights of nn.Linear(784, 128) for a minibatch \(X\) of \(n\) flattened images: entry \((i,j)\) of the output is image \(i\) times neuron \(j\)’s weights, plus entry \(j\) of \(b\).


Each output row comes from one image, just as each row of \(Xw\) came from one observation in the linear models chapter. PyTorch stores the transpose: layer.weight is \(W^T\), with shape [128, 784], and the layer computes X @ layer.weight.T + layer.bias.
Mathematically, the subsequent nn.ReLU activation function is part of this layer. Separating the specification of the activation function from the linear component in code, however, gives greater flexibility.

title: Neural networks
text:
Output layer
The nn.Linear(128, 5) layer is the output layer. It maps the 128 hidden neurons to five output classes. Mathematically, the nn.Softmax(dim=1) activation function is also part of this layer.
What does nn.Softmax do? It normalises, in a particular way, an input vector \(z\) (represented as a tensor of course) into a discrete probability distribution vector \(p\) of the same dimension: \[
\text{Softmax}: z \mapsto p
\] where \(z\) and \(p\) are vectors of the same length, and \(p\) sums to one. Hence here we get a probability vector with five entries. Note that our \(z\) vector (tensor) here has a column for each output class, and hence we normalise over the column dimension, dim=1 (see e.g. torchsummary).
Interestingly, in contrast to most activation functions, this function is not applied separately to each pre-activation neuron value. Instead, the softmax function depends on the values of all elements of the vector given, as its job is to ensure the values together sum to one. It is defined by: \[
\text{Softmax}(z)_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_j{\exp(z_j)}}
\]
Softmax is usually only used for output layers, to provide a final probability distribution over a collection of discrete classes. It is rarely used ‘inside’ neural networks, i.e. in hidden layers, where elementwise activation functions are common.
Finally, although Softmax is conceptually important, it turns out that, for multi-class classification, it is generally better practice to use the LogSoftmax function, nn.LogSoftmax(dim=1), instead of Softmax. And rather than a sum of squared errors, for multi-class classification this last output layer is usually used with a so-called negative log likelihood loss, nn.NLLLoss() that takes in log-probabilities. Equivalently, we can leave out the final activation and use nn.CrossEntropyLoss, which combines LogSoftmax and NLLLoss; most PyTorch examples do this.
Why this loss? The labels are categories, so a squared error on the label numbers doesn’t make sense: it would treat a 7 as closer to an 8 than to a 1. Instead we choose the weights that make the observed labels most probable. The likelihood is the probability the model gives the labels we observed. Treating the images as independent, it is the product \(L=\prod_i p_i\), where \(p_i\) is the predicted probability of image \(i\)’s correct class; for example, probabilities 0.9, 0.6 and 0.2 for three images give \(L=0.108\). Choosing the weights to maximise \(L\) is maximum likelihood estimation. In practice we minimise the negative log-likelihood, \(-\log L=-\sum_i\log p_i\) (natural log), averaged over the images:

the log turns the product into a sum, so the loss is an average over images, like the mean squared error, and a minibatch’s average estimates it;
a product of many probabilities underflows to zero in floating point (for example \(0.9^{60\,000}\)), while the sum of their logs does not;
the log is increasing, so the same weights maximise \(L\) and minimise \(-\log L\).

Each image contributes \(-\log p_i\), which is zero when \(p_i=1\) and grows without bound as \(p_i\to0\), so giving the correct class a low probability costs the most. (Least squares is also maximum likelihood, for independent Gaussian errors with constant variance.)

title: Neural networks
text:
Loading data in PyTorch
Let’s look at an example. The machine learning and computer vision communities have collected many benchmark datasets over the years, and have run numerous competitions based on such datasets. (Interestingly, Donoho has argued that such practices have been central to the successes of data science and machine learning).
A classic example dataset is the handwritten digit-recognition dataset called MNIST. This is a dataset of \(28 \times 28\) images of handwritten digits with 60,000 training images and 10,000 testing images. LeCun et al. (original page, archived) describe this as

a good database for people who want to try learning techniques and pattern recognition methods on real-world data while spending minimal efforts on preprocessing and formatting.

The PyTorch module torchvision contains useful datasets, models, and image transformations for computer vision (image/video machine learning) applications. There are ‘built-in’ datasets in the module torchvision.datasets, which also contains tools (functions, classes etc.) for working with custom datasets. We can load the MNIST dataset as follows:

import torch
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
# Define transformations to be applied to loaded images
# Here just a conversion to tensor format.
transform = transforms.ToTensor()
# Load training and test datasets
train_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=True, 
                transform=transform, download=True)
test_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=False,
                transform=transform, download=True)

The above looks for a local ‘data’ folder. If it doesn’t exist it creates this and downloads the dataset from public sources.

In the tensors chapter we converted the cat image to a PyTorch tensor by hand, with torch.from_numpy, division by 255 and permute. The transform transforms.ToTensor(), which takes no arguments, does the same in one step:

import imageio.v3 as iio
img_arr = iio.imread('./data/cat3.png')  # height, width, channels
# by hand: floats in [0, 1], then channels first

Each MNIST image therefore becomes a tensor of shape [1, 28, 28] with values between 0 and 1:

# one image after ToTensor

torch.Size([1, 28, 28]) torch.float32 0.0 1.0


Here .item() turns a one-element tensor into a plain Python number. A Dataset like this can be indexed, train_dataset[i], and has a length, len(train_dataset). That is all a DataLoader needs to produce minibatches.

title: Neural networks
text:
Normalising the data
It is common to normalise the inputs, for example to have zero mean and unit standard deviation. transforms.Normalize does this, but we supply the mean and standard deviation ourselves, computed beforehand from the training images only:

pixels = train_dataset.data.float() / 255  # scaled to [0, 1]
print(round(pixels.mean().item(), 4), round(pixels.std().item(), 4))

0.1307 0.3081


transforms.Normalize(mean, std) subtracts mean and divides by std, with one value per channel. It goes in the transform argument of datasets.MNIST, combined with ToTensor by transforms.Compose:

# first convert to a tensor, then compute (x - mean) / std
transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,))])
train_normalised = datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=True,
                                  transform=transform)

Compose applies the transforms in the order listed. Normalize works on tensors, so it must come after ToTensor. Across the training images, the normalised pixels then have mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
Using only the training images follows the same rule as data splitting for choosing \(\lambda\) in the previous chapter: the validation and test data should not inform how we fit the model. In this chapter we skip normalisation for simplicity.

title: Neural networks
section: Validation splits and our own data
text:
Validation splits and our own data
To choose hyperparameters such as the learning rate or the number of epochs, we hold out part of the training data as a validation set, for example with torch.utils.data.random_split:

train_part, val_part = torch.utils.data.random_split(
    train_dataset, [50000, 10000])
print(len(train_part), len(val_part))

50000 10000


For data we already have as tensors, such as inputs X and targets y from an experiment, torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X, y) makes a dataset that a DataLoader can use in the same way.

title: Neural networks
text:
Mini-batching the data
For various reasons, modern neural network models usually process data in small batches called minibatches rather than all at once. Each step then needs only part of the data in memory, and in practice minibatch training has often been found to generalise well; the randomness in each minibatch’s gradient is one suggested reason.
Terminology can be inconsistent, but in general, we call the full dataset the batch, and subsets of the dataset minibatches. PyTorch, though, uses ‘batch’ for the minibatch being processed, as in the batch_size argument of DataLoader below. Given an original indexing \(i\) of data points, we shuffle them into a new order \(i'\) and cut this into a partition \(\mathcal{B}\) of minibatches \(B_1,\dots,B_{mb}\), where \(mb\) is the number of minibatches. For example:





The module torch.utils.data has a tool DataLoader that feeds a dataset to the training loop one minibatch at a time. A Dataset says how to get item \(i\); a DataLoader decides which items, in what order and how many at a time. It takes a dataset, a batch_size and a shuffle option.

train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_dataset,
                                batch_size=64,shuffle=True)

The returned object train_loader is a Python iterable – an object that can return its members (here, minibatches) one at a time, and hence be ‘iterated over’, e.g.:

for mb_imgs, mb_labels in train_loader:

If shuffle is true, the dataset is shuffled once at the beginning of each new iteration over the DataLoader. For large datasets, such as images read from disk, the num_workers option lets it prepare minibatches in parallel while the model trains.
A small example shows what a DataLoader does. Each time round a for loop it takes the next few items and stacks them into tensors; the last minibatch holds what is left over:

from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
data = torch.tensor([10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16])  # 7 data points
loader = DataLoader(data, batch_size=3)
for minibatch in loader:
    print(minibatch)

tensor([10, 11, 12])
tensor([13, 14, 15])
tensor([16])


For MNIST each item is an (image, label) pair, so each minibatch is a pair too: a tensor of 64 images and a tensor of their 64 labels. Here we look at just the first minibatch:

for images, labels in train_loader:
    print(images.shape, labels.shape, labels.dtype)
    break  # just look at the first minibatch

torch.Size([64, 1, 28, 28]) torch.Size([64]) torch.int64


The labels are integer class indices, the form the classification loss below expects.

title: Neural networks
section: Batch, minibatch and stochastic gradient descent
text:
Batch, minibatch and stochastic gradient descent
The above leads to three variations of gradient descent:

Batch (full-batch) gradient descent

Minibatch gradient descent

Stochastic gradient descent

The first uses the full dataset at each iteration of gradient descent, the second uses a minibatch for each iteration of gradient descent, and the last uses a single data point. Note: PyTorch uses optim.SGD for all versions of gradient descent; the difference comes from what data you pass it at each iteration.
The basic training process is to randomly divide the training set into minibatches (possibly being the full batch or single data points). Then we fix the shuffled order and iterate through the batches until all data points have been seen. This is called an epoch. We then re-shuffle the data and divide into new minibatches and continue for some number of epochs. The full dataset will hence be ‘seen’ the same number of times as there are epochs. The total number of gradient descent steps will be the number of epochs times the number of minibatches the dataset is divided into at each epoch.
For example, MNIST has 60,000 training images. With batch_size=32 there are \(60\,000/32=1875\) minibatches per epoch, so 10 epochs take \(10\times1875=18\,750\) steps. If the minibatch size does not divide the number of points, round up: with batch_size=64, \(60\,000/64=937.5\), giving 938 minibatches per epoch (937 full and one of 32), which is len(train_loader).
This is illustrated below \(\dots\)

title: Neural networks
section: Training the neural network in PyTorch
text:
Training the neural network in PyTorch
Let’s put it all together!

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

# Define the model with explicit LogSoftmax
num_classes = 10  # For MNIST dataset
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, num_classes),
    nn.LogSoftmax(dim=1)
)
# Define transformations (simple conversion to tensor)
transform = transforms.ToTensor()

# Load datasets
train_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='data', train=True,
                        transform=transform, download=True)
test_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='data', train=False,
                        transform=transform)

# Data loaders
batch_size = 32  # Adjust as needed
train_loader = DataLoader(dataset=train_dataset, 
                            batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
test_loader = DataLoader(dataset=test_dataset, 
                            batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False)


# Loss function and optimiser
criterion = nn.NLLLoss()
optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
# Training loop
num_epochs = 10  # Adjust as needed
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    epoch_loss = 0.0
    for mb_data, mb_targets in train_loader:
        # Zero the gradients
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        # Forward pass
        outputs = model(mb_data)
        # Compute minibatch loss
        mb_loss = criterion(outputs, mb_targets)
        # Accumulate epoch loss (use .item() to get scalar)
        epoch_loss += mb_loss.item()
        # Backward pass and optimization
        mb_loss.backward()

    # Compute average loss per minibatch

    # display
    print(f'Epoch [{epoch+1}/{num_epochs}], '
          f'Average (Per Minibatch) Loss: {avg_epoch_loss:.4f}')

title: Neural networks
section: Example architecture improvements: convolutional neural networks
text:
Example architecture improvements: convolutional neural networks
We have previously mentioned convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as a biology/physics-inspired neural network architecture. Briefly, a convolution kernel is a small ‘patch shaped’ tensor of weights that can be applied to local patches of an image (or video or time-series, for appropriate definitions of ‘patch’) by multiplying the weights of the kernel with the values of each patch, illustrated in the below figure:  This is a special type of linear operation, to be passed into subsequent nonlinear activation functions. For example, the below snippet manually applies an edge-detection kernel of dimensions 3 by 3, which responds to horizontal edges, to the patches of a cat image using torch.einsum (which can apply linear operations like convolution to tensors without flattening).

title: Neural networks
text:
Manual convolution

# kernel for vertical changes in brightness (horizontal edges)
kernel = torch.tensor([[ -1,-2,  -1],
                       [ 0,  0,   0],
                       [ 1,  2,   1]],dtype=torch.float32)

padded_cat = F.pad(cat, pad=(1, 1, 1, 1), 
                    mode='constant', value=0)
patches = padded_cat.unfold(1, 3, 1).unfold(2, 3, 1)

filtered_cat = torch.abs(torch.einsum('cijkl,kl->cij', 
                                       patches, kernel))










In deep learning, the above result is called the convolution of the image and the kernel (strictly, it is a cross-correlation, since the kernel isn’t flipped; nn.Conv2d computes the same thing). PyTorch implements convolution directly, as we see next.

title: Neural networks
text:
Convolutional layers in PyTorch
Each output pixel is the sum of the kernel weights multiplied by the \(3\times3\) patch of the padded image around that pixel, exactly as our unfold and einsum code computed. Each output depends only on nearby pixels (locality), and the same kernel weights are used at every position (weight sharing), so a pattern is detected wherever it appears in the image. These are assumptions about images built into the architecture: an inductive bias, in the terms of the first chapter.
nn.Conv2d, and its function form F.conv2d, compute this directly. F.conv2d expects a minibatch of images with shape (batch, channels, height, width) and kernels with shape (output channels, input channels, height, width). The cat has shape (3, height, width), so cat.unsqueeze(1) inserts a channel dimension of size 1, treating each colour channel as a separate grayscale image, and kernel.view(1, 1, 3, 3) gives the kernel one input and one output channel. squeeze(1) removes the extra dimension again, and torch.allclose checks that two tensors agree to within a small tolerance. The result matches the patch-based calculation above, up to rounding error:

same = F.conv2d(cat.unsqueeze(1), kernel.view(1, 1, 3, 3), padding=1)
print(torch.allclose(same.squeeze(1).abs(), filtered_cat, atol=1e-6))

True


In a network the kernels are learned. A layer nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride, padding) takes:

in_channels: the number of channels in each input image, 1 for grayscale and 3 for colour;
out_channels: the number of output channels (often called feature maps), each from its own learned kernel;
kernel_size: the height and width of each kernel, e.g. 3 for \(3\times3\);
stride: the step between kernel positions (default 1);
padding: the number of zero rows and columns added around the border (default 0).

It has one kernel for each pair of input and output channels, plus a bias for each output channel:

conv = nn.Conv2d(1, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
print(conv.weight.shape, sum(p.numel() for p in conv.parameters()))
print(conv(torch.rand(64, 1, 28, 28)).shape)

torch.Size([8, 1, 3, 3]) 80
torch.Size([64, 8, 28, 28])


Eight \(3\times3\) kernels and their biases make 80 parameters, whereas an nn.Linear layer from the 784 pixels to 784 outputs has \(784\times784+784=615\,440\). For an input of height \(H\), a kernel of size \(k\), padding \(p\) and stride \(s\), the output height is \(\lfloor(H+2p-k)/s\rfloor+1\), and similarly for the width; here \((28+2-3)/1+1=28\).

title: Neural networks
text:
Pooling and a small CNN
A pooling layer summarises each small block of a feature map by a single number. Max pooling, nn.MaxPool2d(2), keeps the largest value in each \(2\times2\) block, while average pooling, nn.AvgPool2d(2), keeps the mean. By default the blocks don’t overlap (the stride equals the block size), so the height and width halve:



Max pooling with \(2\times2\) blocks: each shaded block of the feature map is replaced by its largest value, shown in bold.



# one image, one channel, 4 x 4
x = torch.tensor([[[[1., 3., 2., 0.],
                    [4., 2., 1., 1.],
                    [0., 1., 5., 6.],
                    [3., 2., 7., 8.]]]])
print(nn.MaxPool2d(2)(x))

tensor([[[[4., 2.],
          [3., 8.]]]])


Pooling has no parameters. It makes the feature maps smaller, so later layers need fewer weights, and it makes the output less sensitive to a feature moving by a pixel within its block.
Stacking convolution, activation and pooling, then flattening into a linear layer, gives a small convolutional neural network (CNN) for MNIST:

cnn = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(1, 8, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool2d(2),                            # 8 x 14 x 14
    nn.Conv2d(8, 16, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool2d(2),                            # 16 x 7 x 7
    nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(16 * 7 * 7, 10), nn.LogSoftmax(dim=1)
)
print(sum(p.numel() for p in cnn.parameters()))

9098


Because the convolutions share their weights, this network has 9,098 parameters, against 101,770 for the fully connected network we trained above. In Lab 5 we build and train LeNet-5, an early CNN for digit recognition, and compare it with the fully connected network.

title: Neural networks
section: Physics-informed neural networks: hybrid neural models
text:
Physics-informed neural networks: hybrid neural models
In the next chapter, we combine a neural network with a physics-based loss term, giving a hybrid neural model, or physics-informed neural network.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
From hybrid linear to hybrid neural models
In the hybrid linear models section we represented a time series on a fine time grid with a spline data model, \(y=Bw\), linked it to the observations with an observation matrix \(A_{\text{obs}}\), and fitted it by minimising a data loss plus \(\lambda\) times a penalty on a differential equation. We represented the derivatives in the differential equation with finite-difference matrices, such as \(D\) in \(DBw\). A hybrid neural model keeps this structure and changes two things:
Note that we could make either change without the other, e.g. we could apply difference matrices to a network’s predictions on the fine grid. Both data models are functions of \(t\) with weights fitted to data. The spline is a weighted sum of fixed basis functions, so its predictions are linear in \(w\), and we fitted it with one least-squares solve. A network’s predictions are nonlinear in its weights, so we minimise the loss by gradient descent instead, as in the neural networks section.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Hybrid linear model
Hybrid neural model




Data model

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Pendulum revisited
Recall that the angular motion \(\theta(t)\) of a pendulum with length \(l\) subject to Newton’s laws and no friction or air resistance, is given by \[
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{g}{l}\sin \theta = 0
\] with initial conditions \[
\theta(0) = \theta_0,\ \ \frac{d\theta}{dt}(0) = v_0
\] A schematic is shown below.





The small angle approximation uses \(\sin \theta \approx \theta\), giving the linear pendulum model: \[
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{g}{l}\theta = 0
\] with the same initial conditions.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Predicting the pendulum
Now, let’s consider a variation on our original pendulum prediction problem. Suppose we have \(M\) (possibly noisy) observations of the form \[(t_i,\theta_i),\ i=1,\dots,M\] from a nonlinear pendulum and wish to predict \(\theta_j\) for a collection of new, future \(t_j\) values \[(t_j,\theta_j),\ j=M+1,\dots,M+K\]
For example, below we show the observed data in blue, the future (not yet seen) data in red, and the true, unobserved angle trajectory in black. Here the pendulum is released from rest at \(160^\circ\) and observed every 0.2 s up to \(t=5\), with noise of standard deviation 0.1.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Two time grids, two losses
As in our discussion of hybrid linear models, we again have two time grids: a fine time grid associated with the underlying physical process (as governed by the ODE/Newton’s Laws), and a coarse time grid associated with our observations of the physical process. (Reality may of course involve continuous time physics but here we use a very fine grid as a proxy for this.) In the hybrid linear model, the fine grid also set the spacing of the difference matrices, and so the accuracy of the derivatives. With a neural network, automatic differentiation gives the time derivatives exactly at any \(t\), as we’ll see, so the fine grid is just the set of times at which we check the ODE.
These two time grids naturally lead to two types of loss functions: a data loss associated with the observations, and a physics loss associated with the underlying physical process. First, we will consider the data loss.
If we denote the ‘underlying’ angular motion defined on the fine time grid, \(t_{\text{fine}}\), by \(\theta_{\text{fine}}\), and our observations of the angular motion on the coarse time grid, \(t_{\text{obs}}\), by \(\theta_{\text{obs}}\), we can (conceptually at least) use an observation matrix \(A_{\text{obs}}\) to relate the variables on the two grids: \[
t_{\text{obs}} = A_{\text{obs}}t_{\text{fine}},\ \ \theta_{\text{obs}} = A_{\text{obs}}\theta_{\text{fine}}.
\] Rather than directly enforce the physics right now, we will first assume that the fine-scale dynamics can be approximated by a neural network model: \[
\theta_{\text{fine}}= f_{\text{NN}}(t_{\text{fine}};w),
\] where \(w\) are the parameters (weights and biases) of the neural network, and \(f_{\text{NN}}(t_{\text{fine}};w)\) represents the vector of predictions at the fine time grid \(t_{\text{fine}}\). We explicitly represent the fine-scale dynamics here because we ultimately want to predict the angular motion at times we have not observed.
These elements lead to a data loss term that, for fixed data, depends on the neural network parameters and takes a form such as: \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{loss}_{\text{data}}(w) &= \frac{1}{M}\|\theta_{\text{obs}}-A_{\text{obs}}f_{\text{NN}}(t_{\text{fine}};w)\|^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{M}\|\theta_{\text{obs}}-f_{\text{NN}}(t_{\text{obs}};w)\|^2
\end{aligned}
\] where \(M\) is the number of observations, which we may or may not divide by (dividing by \(M\) doesn’t change which \(w\) minimises the data loss on its own, but it does change the balance with the physics loss below, and so what a given \(\lambda\) means).

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Physics loss and time derivatives
We will consider the neural network model in more detail shortly. First we consider, at a high level, how to construct the physics loss, and in particular how to evaluate the derivatives in the ODE on the fine time grid.
In the hybrid linear model, a finite-difference matrix \(D\) mapped the spline’s values on the fine grid to approximate derivatives, \(DBw\). Here we use PyTorch’s automatic differentiation (its autograd engine) instead, which gives the exact derivative of the network’s prediction with respect to time.
We have used automatic differentiation before, in the computation graphs part of Week 2 and to train models since, but always to get the derivative of a loss with respect to a model’s parameters, which loss.backward() computed by working back through the recorded calculation and then added to each parameter’s .grad. The physics loss instead needs the derivative of the model’s prediction with respect to its input, time. PyTorch computes this from the same recorded calculation and with the same chain rule, since as far as PyTorch is concerned the weights, biases and times are all just tensors with requires_grad=True. The only differences are in which derivative we ask for and how we then use it. To handle these we need three new ideas, which we’ll take in turn using simple functions whose derivatives we already know:

getting a derivative with respect to time back as a tensor;
getting the derivative at every time at once;
differentiating that derivative again.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Derivatives with respect to time
Let’s start with a derivative at a single time. Like backward() in Week 2, torch.autograd.grad differentiates a single number, so consider \(y=\sin t\) at \(t=1\), where the derivative should be \(\cos 1=0.5403\). As for the parameter \(x\) in Week 2, we set requires_grad=True on t so that PyTorch records the operations that use it. (We didn’t need to do this for the network in Week 5, because by default PyTorch sets requires_grad=True on a network’s weights and biases when it creates them.)

t = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.sin(t)
print(torch.autograd.grad(y, t))
print(t.grad)

(tensor(0.5403),)
None


torch.autograd.grad computes the derivative from the recorded calculation in the same way as backward(), but returns it rather than adding it to .grad, which is why t.grad is still None. The first argument of grad (outputs) is what we differentiate, and the second (inputs) is what we differentiate with respect to. Since we could list several tensors as inputs, the result is a tuple with one derivative for each, and so here, with just one input, we take the tuple’s first element, [0].
We use grad for the time derivatives because we need them as part of the next calculation, the ODE residual. If we used backward() on a network’s prediction instead, it would also add derivatives to the .grad of every weight and bias, and the optimiser would then use these in its update. We still use loss.backward() for the derivative of the total loss with respect to the weights and biases, though, since the optimiser reads it from their .grad.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Derivatives at many times
Now let’s move from one time to a grid of times. On the fine grid, a function \(y(t)\) becomes a vector of values \(y_i=y(t_i)\), and its time derivative becomes another vector. In the hybrid linear model, the difference matrix \(D\) mapped the vector of values to the slopes of the lines through neighbouring points, while automatic differentiation treats each \(t_i\) as a separate number and gives the slope of the tangent at each point, \(y'(t_i)\). The figure below shows both for \(y=\sin t\) on a coarse grid, with times 1 apart.









The physics loss needs the derivative at every fine-grid time, but grad only differentiates a single number. One trick for getting the derivatives at all the grid points at once is to differentiate the sum of the entries. To see why this works, take a function \(y(t)\) at three times \(t_1,t_2,t_3\), with \(y_i=y(t_i)\) and sum \(S=y_1+y_2+y_3\). For \(y(t)=t^2\) we get:

t = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
y = t**2
print(torch.autograd.grad(y.sum(), t)[0])

tensor([2., 4., 6.])


Here t is a single tensor holding three numbers, but PyTorch treats each entry as a separate variable, so entry \(i\) of the result is \(\partial S/\partial t_i\). Since t**2 squares each entry separately, only \(y_i\) depends on \(t_i\), and so \(\partial S/\partial t_i=y'(t_i)=2t_i\), i.e. 2, 4 and 6 here. The same is true for our network, since each time is a separate row of its input and each layer acts on each row separately, giving \(\theta_i=f_{\text{NN}}(t_i;w)\).
In the hybrid linear models section we applied a difference matrix to \(y=\sin t\) at 100 times between 0 and 12. The same trick gives the derivative at all 100 times:

t = torch.linspace(0, 12, 100, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.sin(t)
dy_dt = torch.autograd.grad(y.sum(), t)[0]

The top plot compares the two ways of getting the derivative of \(\sin t\) with the exact derivative, \(\cos t\), and the bottom plot shows their errors. The difference matrix gives approximations at all but the first time, with errors up to about 0.06 here (the times are 0.12 apart). Automatic differentiation gives \(\cos t\) at all 100 times, up to rounding.









What if an output depends on more than one input? A cumulative sum is a simple example, since output \(i\) adds up inputs \(1,\dots,i\):

x = torch.linspace(0, 1, 5, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.cumsum(x, 0)   # each output adds up the inputs so far
print(torch.autograd.grad(y.sum(), x)[0])

tensor([5., 4., 3., 2., 1.])


Each \(dy_i/dx_i\) is 1, but the result is not all ones. It is still the derivative of the sum \(S\), but now entry \(i\) is \(\sum_j \partial y_j/\partial x_i\), which adds up the effect of \(x_i\) on every output that includes it. This reduces to \(dy_i/dx_i\) only when each output depends on its own input alone. Our network has no dependence between times, so for the network the sum does give the derivative at every time.
The sum is in fact a special case of the grad_outputs argument of grad, which lets us give a weight \(v_i\) to each output \(y_i\). PyTorch then differentiates the weighted sum \(\sum_i v_iy_i\), and our sum \(S\) corresponds to setting every weight to 1, which is how other code often writes the call. backward() can give the same derivatives too, adding them to t.grad and taking the same weights through its argument gradient:

t = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
print(torch.autograd.grad(t**2, t, grad_outputs=torch.ones(3))[0])
(t**2).sum().backward()   # the same derivatives, added to t.grad
print(t.grad)

tensor([2., 4., 6.])
tensor([2., 4., 6.])

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Differentiating a derivative: create_graph=True
The ODE also needs the second derivative, \(d^2\theta/dt^2\). In the hybrid linear model we got this by multiplying difference matrices together, and here we instead call grad again, this time on the first derivative. However, to differentiate the first derivative, PyTorch needs a record of how it was calculated from \(t\), in the same way as it records the forward calculation, and by default it doesn’t keep one. For example, for \(y=t^3\) the derivative \(3t^2\) comes back from grad as plain numbers, with no record of how they depend on \(t\). Setting create_graph=True tells PyTorch to also record the derivative calculation, so that we can differentiate the result again:

t = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
y = t**3
dy_dt = torch.autograd.grad(y.sum(), t, create_graph=True)[0]
print(dy_dt)
d2y_dt2 = torch.autograd.grad(dy_dt.sum(), t)[0]
print(d2y_dt2)

tensor([ 3., 12., 27.], grad_fn=<MulBackward0>)
tensor([ 6., 12., 18.])


These are \(3t^2\) and \(6t\) at \(t=1,2,3\), and the grad_fn in the first printout is PyTorch’s record of the operation that produced dy_dt. Without create_graph=True, dy_dt prints as tensor([ 3., 12., 27.]), with no grad_fn, and the second call fails with RuntimeError: element 0 of tensors does not require grad and does not have a grad_fn. (Note that Week 2’s retain_graph=True doesn’t help here, since it only keeps the saved forward values for a second backward pass through the same calculation, and doesn’t record the derivative calculation.)
Training needs create_graph=True for a second reason. The physics loss is computed from the time derivatives, which themselves depend on the weights, so when loss.backward() differentiates the physics loss with respect to the weights it has to work back through the derivative calculation too, and that needs a record of it. We can see this with a model that has a single weight \(a\), \(\theta(t)=\sin(at)\), so that \(d\theta/dt=a\cos(at)\), and the loss \(L=(d\theta/dt)^2\), which, like the physics loss, is built from the time derivative. By the chain rule and the product rule, \[
\frac{dL}{da}=2\,\frac{d\theta}{dt}\,\frac{d}{da}\Big(\frac{d\theta}{dt}\Big)=2a\cos(at)\big(\cos(at)-at\sin(at)\big),
\] which is \(-0.6509\) at \(a=2\) and \(t=0.5\). PyTorch gives the same:

a = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)    # one weight
t = torch.tensor([0.5], requires_grad=True)  # one time
theta = torch.sin(a * t)
dtheta_dt = torch.autograd.grad(theta.sum(), t, create_graph=True)[0]
loss = torch.mean(dtheta_dt**2)   # mean, as in the physics loss
loss.backward()
print(a.grad)

tensor(-0.6509)


Without create_graph=True in the grad call, dtheta_dt has no record of how it depends on \(a\), and loss.backward() fails with the same error. We could also have used torch.autograd.grad(loss, a) here, which returns the same value.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Constructing the physics loss
Given the ability to compute time derivatives in PyTorch, we can do this for the neural network model \(f_{\text{NN}}(t_{\text{fine}};w)\), and then use these derivatives to construct the physics loss. This will have the general form:

import torch
import torch.autograd as autograd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
# e.g. 100 times, one per row (nn.Linear(1, 50) needs [100, 1])
t_fine = torch.linspace(0,10,100,requires_grad=True).unsqueeze(1)
theta_fine_pred = model(t_fine)

# Compute first derivative dtheta/dt
# note: grad always returns a tuple of gradients, 
# even if only one, so take first element
dtheta_dt_fine = torch.autograd.grad(
    outputs=theta_fine_pred.sum(),
    inputs=t_fine,
    create_graph=True
)[0] 
    
# Compute second derivative d2theta/dt2
d2theta_dt2 = torch.autograd.grad(
    outputs=dtheta_dt_fine.sum(),
    inputs=t_fine,
    create_graph=True
)[0]

Here torch.linspace gives a tensor of shape [100], and .unsqueeze(1) adds a second dimension of size 1, giving shape [100, 1], with one time per row, as nn.Linear(1, 50) expects.
Both calls need create_graph=True: the first so that the second call can differentiate dtheta_dt_fine, and the second because the physics loss is computed from d2theta_dt2, so in training loss.backward() needs a record of how d2theta_dt2 depends on the weights.
Assuming the ODE holds at every fine-grid time, the physics loss for the network has the form \[
\text{loss}_{\text{physics}}(w) = \frac{1}{P}\|\frac{\partial^2 f_{\text{NN}}(t_{\text{fine}};w)}{\partial t^2} + \frac{g}{l}\sin f_{\text{NN}}(t_{\text{fine}};w)\|^2
\] where \(P\) is the number of fine-grid times.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Combining the losses
The overall loss function is then a combination of the data loss and the physics loss: \[
\text{loss}_{\text{total}}(w) = \text{loss}_{\text{data}}(w) + \lambda\times\text{loss}_{\text{physics}}(w)
\] where \(\lambda\) is a hyperparameter that weights the relative importance of the data and physics terms.
As for the linear model, \(\lambda\) can be chosen by using a simple hold-out validation set, a more sophisticated method such as cross-validation, or set by the user based on external knowledge. Since we want to predict forward in time, the validation observations should be the latest ones (a chronological split, as in the hybrid linear models chapter). Here we just manually set (by trial and error…) \(\lambda\) for simplicity.
We’re almost ready to put this all together, but first let’s consider the neural network model in a bit more detail.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Simple neural network model
Here is a simple example of a neural network model in PyTorch, with two hidden layers and tanh activation functions. We use tanh here because it is smooth (infinitely differentiable) which tends to be appropriate for ODE models (requiring derivatives in time), cf. ReLU which is technically not smooth and more common in classification tasks. ReLU is linear on each side of zero and the network’s other layers are linear, so a ReLU network’s output is piecewise linear in its input, here \(t\). Its second derivative with respect to \(t\), which the physics loss needs, is therefore zero almost everywhere.
We will again use torch.nn.Sequential to define the model:

import torch.nn as nn
nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(1, 50),
        nn.Tanh(),
        nn.Linear(50, 50),
        nn.Tanh(),
        nn.Linear(50, 1)
        )

This has a single input neuron (representing time), two hidden layers with 50 neurons each, and a single output neuron (representing the angular motion). The nn.Linear layers are fully connected layers, and the nn.Tanh layers are the activation functions.
The input is a single scalar ‘feature’ \(t\) and the output is a single scalar ‘response’ \(\theta(t)\). As with our other models, we can evaluate this model for a collection of input values, e.g. at \(t_{\text{obs}}\) or \(t_{\text{fine}}\), to get a collection of output values. Each evaluation is like a ‘row’ of a linear model, though now we have a nonlinear model, and PyTorch evaluates all the rows (the batch dimension) at once.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Putting it all together
We can now put all these elements together to construct a hybrid neural model for the pendulum motion. We assume that the data has been generated already as above.
In contrast to the linear example (a projectile), the physics here is nonlinear: we generate the data with the nonlinear pendulum equation and use the same equation in the physics loss, so the physics model is ‘perfect’. A linear model can’t use this equation directly, since \(\sin\theta\) makes the problem nonlinear in the weights. We could still fit a spline model with this equation by nonlinear least squares, which repeatedly linearises the problem and solves a least-squares problem like those in the hybrid linear models section at each step. The network’s loss is nonlinear in its weights anyway, so this is no harder. We could also try the linear pendulum equation in the physics loss, i.e. an imperfect physics model.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# NN parameters
torch.manual_seed(0)
lambda_reg = 1.5e-3  # Regularization parameter λ
num_epochs = 10000  # Number of training epochs

# Define the neural network model using nn.Sequential
model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(1, 50),
        nn.Tanh(),
        nn.Linear(50, 50),
        nn.Tanh(),
        nn.Linear(50, 1)
        )

# Set up the optimizer
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)


# Convert t_data, t_grid and y_data to torch.float32, once
# (unsqueeze adds a dimension: one time per row)
t_data_tensor = torch.tensor(t_data,
        dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)
t_grid_tensor = torch.tensor(t_grid,
        dtype=torch.float32,
        requires_grad=True).unsqueeze(1)
y_data_tensor = torch.tensor(y_data, dtype=torch.float32)

# Training loop
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Compute the model predictions at observation points
    y_pred_obs = model(t_data_tensor)
    # Compute the data loss
    data_loss = torch.mean((
        y_pred_obs.squeeze() - y_data_tensor) ** 2) 
    
    # Compute the model predictions at fine grid 
    y_pred_grid = model(t_grid_tensor)
    # Compute first derivative dy/dt on fine grid
    dy_dt = torch.autograd.grad(
        outputs=y_pred_grid.sum(),
        inputs=t_grid_tensor,
        create_graph=True
    )[0]
    # Compute second derivative d2y/dt2
    d2y_dt2 = torch.autograd.grad(
        outputs=dy_dt.sum(),
        inputs=t_grid_tensor,
        create_graph=True
    )[0]


    # Define the ODE residual
    ode_residual = d2y_dt2 + g_true/l_true*torch.sin(y_pred_grid)

    # Compute the physics loss
    physics_loss = torch.mean(ode_residual ** 2)
    
    # Total loss
    loss = data_loss + lambda_reg * physics_loss

    # Backward pass and optimization
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

The loop uses both kinds of derivative from the previous sections. The two torch.autograd.grad calls give the first and second time derivatives for the ODE residual, and loss.backward() then gives the derivative of the total loss with respect to the weights and biases, working back through those time derivatives, and adds it to each parameter’s .grad. As in Week 2, optimizer.step() uses these to update the parameters we gave the optimiser, model.parameters(), and optimizer.zero_grad() clears them at the start of the next pass. (loss.backward() also adds a derivative to the .grad of the tensor of times, since we created it with requires_grad=True, but nothing uses it because the optimiser only updates the weights and biases.)
Each pass through the loop uses all the observations and all the fine-grid times, so this is full-batch gradient descent. As with the images in Week 5, we could instead split the fine-grid times into minibatches, with one step for each minibatch.
Result:









The network fits the data well, but after about \(t=7\) the prediction stops swinging and sits at \(\theta\approx-\pi\), i.e. the pendulum balanced upside down. Why does it end up there? The ODE on its own has many solutions, including every swing of the pendulum and constants such as \(\theta=0\) (at rest) and \(\theta=-\pi\), which satisfy the ODE exactly because \(\sin\theta=0\) and the second derivative is zero. Initial conditions would pick out one of these, but the physics loss doesn’t include any. Up to \(t=5\) the data play that role and select the swinging solution, but after the last observation nothing does.
Since the physics loss is only a soft penalty and \(\lambda\) is small, breaking the ODE slightly for a short time (here between about \(t=5\) and \(t=7\)) costs very little, and lets the curve move onto a different solution. Constants are especially easy for training to reach, since they make the residual exactly zero. This is a known difficulty with PINNs: fixed points (equilibria) of a dynamical system, like this one, create local minima in the physics loss that training can get stuck in, especially when the system starts close to one (our pendulum starts at 160°, nearly upside down) or the time interval is long (Rohrhofer et al., 2023).
The same difficulty arises without a neural network. If we use the spline data model from the hybrid linear models section, \(\theta=Bw\), with the same nonlinear physics loss and the same \(\lambda\), the loss is nonlinear in \(w\), and we can fit it by nonlinear least squares, as described above. The figure compares the result with the network’s. Up to \(t=5\) both fit the data. After that the splines keep swinging, but with a smaller amplitude and a shorter period than the true motion, close to another solution of the pendulum equation (a pendulum’s smaller swings are faster). Neither model is pinned to the true motion once the data stop.

title: Hybrid neural models
text:
Takeaways
Notes:

Within the data, both hybrid models, the network and the splines, fit more flexibly than a pure physics model would, closely enough to follow the noise. Beyond the data the physics is enforced only weakly, so the fit can switch to another solution of the ODE. A hybrid model doesn’t by itself solve the extrapolation problem.
Here the physics is exact, and the pure physics model, the pendulum ODE with its initial angle and velocity fitted to the data, extrapolates well, while the hybrid models do less well. A hybrid model is of most use when the physics is only approximately right, particularly within the range of the available data. (Fitting the pure model is also a nonlinear least-squares problem, and from a poor starting guess it can stop at a wrong solution too.)
I found it quite difficult to tune the training parameters for the neural network model! The model was very sensitive to the learning rate, the number of epochs, and the regularisation parameter. I also gave up on SGD and used the Adam optimiser instead! (Adam is a version of gradient descent that adapts the step size for each parameter as it goes. In PyTorch it is used just like optim.SGD.) Even then my results were not really that great.
Changing \(\lambda\) doesn’t simply fix this. With \(\lambda = 0.1\) the swings after \(t=5\) shrink and die away, and with \(\lambda = 1\) the network ignores the data altogether and predicts \(\theta\approx 0\) throughout, i.e. the pendulum at rest, which also satisfies the ODE exactly. The true motion would score better on both losses, so here the loss doesn’t prefer the wrong answer, and training has instead got stuck on an easy solution.
While this may be my own limitations, it is also a common issue with neural networks: they can be difficult to tune and interpret. This is another reason why we included simpler linear models in this course – they are often much easier to interpret and tune. In addition, the same ideas can be extended to nonlinear models using a similar approach to the linear model approach, without the need for neural networks.
Having said that, with more time and effort, neural networks can be very impressive and powerful tools!
